questions.question: Distinguish between top-down and bottom-up development, giving one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
questions.expected_answer: Top-down development is planned by governments, companies or international bodies through large projects (e.g. Lesotho Highlands Water Project, Katse Dam 1998); advantage: provides large infrastructure such as water transfer and power; disadvantages: costly, may displace people, benefits may go to cities or elites, corruption. Bottom-up development is planned by communities (e.g. borehole, cooperative); advantages: cheap, matches local needs, locally maintained, builds skills; disadvantages: small scale, may depend on outside funding.

questions.question: Explain appropriate technology and microfinance as alternatives to industrialisation, with examples.
questions.expected_answer: Appropriate technology (Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful, 1973) is affordable, uses local materials and skills, can be repaired locally and uses little energy: treadle pumps, drip irrigation, solar lanterns, efficient stoves, rainwater tanks, the Hippo Water Roller. Microfinance provides small loans and savings to poor people without collateral, e.g. Grameen Bank (Muhammad Yunus, from 1976; Nobel Peace Prize 2006), lending mainly to women in groups. Stokvels are South African savings clubs. Limits: debt and high interest.

questions.question: Describe two alternative development paths used in South Africa or Africa and evaluate their limitations.
questions.expected_answer: Community-based tourism and ecotourism: the Makuleke community regained about 24 000 hectares in Kruger in 1998 and earns from lodges for schools and bursaries; Working for Water (1995) and EPWP create jobs while restoring the environment; M-Pesa (Kenya, 2007) shows digital leapfrogging; agriculture and cooperatives support smallholders. Limits: tourism collapsed in 2020; small projects cannot employ millions; microfinance can create debt; elites may capture benefits; they work best alongside conventional development.
